tagline: The skin is the body's first line of defense, and the nurse is often the first to see it fail.
overview: Tissue integrity means intact skin, mucous membranes, cornea, and subcutaneous tissue that can protect, sense, regulate temperature, and repair itself. This concept covers normal skin structure and function, how to assess skin across all skin tones, common infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic disorders, how wounds are classified, and the nursing, nutritional, and pharmacologic care that keeps skin healthy across the lifespan.

topics.title: Skin Structure & Function
topics.summary: The skin is the largest organ in the body. Its three layers work together to protect, sense, regulate temperature, and make vitamin D.

sections.heading: The integumentary system
sections.body: The integumentary system includes the skin, hair, nails, and glands (sweat and sebaceous). Tissue integrity is broader than skin alone. It means intact skin, mucous membranes, cornea, and subcutaneous tissue. Impaired tissue integrity is damage to the epidermis and/or dermis, and it may extend deeper. Internal factors (genetics, age, overall health) and external factors (activity, environment, injury) both affect it.

sections.heading: Layers of the skin
bullets: Epidermis (outer, avascular). It is the barrier layer. Keratinocytes make keratin, which makes skin tough and water-resistant. Melanocytes make melanin, which absorbs UV radiation. The epidermis renews itself about every 4 weeks, and the stratum corneum is shed continuously.

Dermis (middle, the “working layer”). It contains collagen and elastin for strength and stretch, plus blood vessels, lymphatics, nerve endings, hair follicles, and sweat and sebaceous glands. The dermis feeds the avascular epidermis.

Subcutaneous tissue / hypodermis (innermost). Technically it is not skin. It is adipose and connective tissue that stores about half of the body's fat, insulates, cushions bony prominences, stores energy, and anchors the skin to muscle and bone.

sections.heading: Functions of the skin
bullets: Protection. It is a physical and chemical barrier against microorganisms, chemicals, trauma, and UV light. The skin's acid mantle (pH about 4.5 to 5.5) discourages bacterial growth.
Sensation. Receptors detect touch, pain, pressure, and temperature.
Thermoregulation. Blood vessels dilate to release heat and constrict to conserve it. Sweat glands cool the body by evaporation.
Excretion. Sweat removes water, salts, and small amounts of urea and other wastes.
Vitamin D synthesis. UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin into a vitamin D precursor, which supports calcium absorption.
Fluid balance and immunity. The skin prevents excessive water loss, and Langerhans cells present antigens.

sections.heading: Lifespan snapshot
sections.body: Infants have thin skin, a large body surface area relative to weight, and immature sweat glands. This means greater heat and fluid loss and greater absorption of topical agents. Adult skin is thicker and well hydrated. Older adults have thinner, less elastic, drier skin with less subcutaneous fat and slower healing.

table.caption: Skin layers at a glance
rows: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells; no blood vessels
Loss of epidermis alone (abrasion, blister) heals by regeneration without a scar
Collagen, elastin, vessels, nerves, glands, follicles
Damage here causes pain and bleeding; deeper dermal loss heals with scar tissue
Insulation and cushioning; loss in older adults ↑ hypothermia and pressure risk

pearls: Any break in the skin means two immediate problems: infection risk and fluid/heat loss. Large skin loss, such as burns, makes both life-threatening.
The epidermis has no blood vessels. A wound that bleeds has reached at least the dermis.
Older adults and clients on long-term corticosteroids have thin dermis. Tape removal alone can cause skin tears.
redFlags: Loss of skin over a large body surface area. Watch for hypovolemia, hypothermia, and sepsis.

topics.title: Skin Assessment & Lesions
topics.summary: Accurate skin assessment across all skin tones depends on knowing where to look, how to palpate, and the right name for what you see.

sections.heading: General skin assessment
sections.body: Inspect in good natural (or non-glare) light and compare both sides. Assess color, temperature, moisture, texture, turgor, edema, and lesions. Check hair and nails too (clubbing, capillary refill, fungal changes). In older adults, test turgor over the sternum or clavicle, not the back of the hand, because loss of elasticity makes hand tenting unreliable. Ask about itching, recent changes, sun exposure, new products, medications, and home remedies.

sections.heading: Assessing darker skin tones
sections.body: Melanin can hide color changes, so rely more on sites with little pigment and on palpation.
bullets: Pallor looks yellow-brown in brown skin and ashen gray in black skin. Check conjunctivae, oral mucosa, and nail beds.
Cyanosis: inspect nail beds, lips, oral (buccal) mucosa, and conjunctivae. Lips and mucosa may look ashen or gray.
Jaundice: look at the sclera (away from the normal pigmented edges), the hard palate, and the palms and soles, not just the skin.

Erythema / inflammation / early pressure injury may look darker (purple, maroon, or deeper brown), taut, shiny, or indurated. Palpate for warmth, edema, induration, or bogginess and compare with the surrounding skin. Lightly moistening the skin can make changes easier to see.
Petechiae are easier to see in the oral mucosa and conjunctivae.
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is common after lesions heal. Melasma, keloids, pseudofolliculitis barbae, and dermatosis papulosa nigra are more common in darker skin.

sections.heading: Classifying skin disorders
sections.body: Skin disorders are hard to classify because symptoms such as itching, redness, and inflammation overlap. Two common systems are acute vs chronic and by type. Acute disorders are short-term with situational causes, such as bacterial infection or dermatitis, and are treated by reducing inflammation and avoiding triggers. Chronic disorders are long-term or lifelong, such as psoriasis or genetic conditions, and treatment aims for remission, not cure. The types are infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic. The skin can also reflect systemic disease. For example, dry coarse skin with hair loss suggests hypothyroidism, jaundice suggests liver disease, and a butterfly rash suggests lupus.

sections.heading: Screening
sections.body: Teach monthly skin self-examination with mirrors in good light. Cover sun-exposed areas (face, ears, neck, scalp, arms, legs) and also the trunk, back, palms, soles, between the toes, and under the nails. Professional full-body exams may include biopsy, cultures, or patch testing.

table.caption: Primary lesions (arise from previously normal skin) and secondary lesions (evolve from primary lesions or trauma)
rows: Flat, non-palpable color change; macule <1 cm, patch >1 cm
Elevated, solid; papule <1 cm, plaque >1 cm (often a flat-topped cluster)
Elevated, firm, deeper; nodule 1–2 cm, tumor >2 cm
Linear crack into dermis / loss of epidermis only (moist, no scar) / loss into dermis or deeper (may scar)
Athlete's foot / ruptured vesicle / stasis ulcer
Fibrous tissue replacing dermis / hypertrophied scar extending beyond wound borders
Healed incision / ear piercing in darker skin

pearls: Memorize the 1 cm cut-off for flat, raised, and fluid lesions: macule→patch, papule→plaque, vesicle→bulla. Nodule vs tumor is 2 cm.
In darker skin, you often can't “see” redness. Palpate for warmth, induration, and pain, and compare with adjacent skin.
Check the conjunctivae, oral mucosa, nail beds, palms, and soles when looking for pallor, cyanosis, or jaundice in clients with dark skin.
Document lesions by type, size (cm), color, shape, distribution, and drainage. “Rash on arm” is not an assessment.
redFlags: Ashen gray lips and oral mucosa with tachycardia or hypotension point to hypoxemia or shock. Act, don't just document.
A new, changing, bleeding, or non-healing lesion needs provider referral.

topics.title: Infectious Skin Disorders
topics.summary: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites cause most skin infections. The nurse's job is to recognize them, contain their spread, and teach.

sections.heading: Bacterial
bullets: Impetigo (Staphylococcus aureus or group A Streptococcus). Vesicles/pustules rupture into honey-colored crusts, usually around the nose and mouth in children. It is very contagious. Use contact precautions. Gently soak and wash crusts off with soap and water, then apply topical mupirocin or give oral antibiotics for widespread disease. Cut the child's nails, use separate towels, and keep the child out of school or daycare until 24 hours after antibiotics start. Strep impetigo can lead to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, so watch for dark (cola-colored) urine and edema.

Cellulitis is a deeper dermal and subcutaneous infection: a spreading, warm, red, tender, edematous area, often on the lower leg, sometimes with fever. Outline the border with a skin marker and note date and time to track spread. Elevate and immobilize the limb, give antibiotics, and monitor temperature and WBC. Report rapid spread, crepitus, pain out of proportion to findings, or bullae, which may mean necrotizing fasciitis.
Folliculitis / furuncles / carbuncles are infected hair follicles. MRSA is a common cause. Don't squeeze them. Warm compresses help, and larger lesions may need incision and drainage.

sections.heading: Viral
bullets: Varicella (chickenpox). A crop of macules → papules → vesicles → crusts, with lesions in all stages at once. The virus spreads through the air and by contact, so use airborne + contact precautions until all lesions are crusted. Treat itching (oatmeal baths, trimmed nails) and avoid aspirin because of the risk of Reye syndrome. The vaccine is live.

Herpes zoster (shingles) is varicella reactivation. It causes a painful unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash. Localized zoster in an immunocompetent client: standard precautions and cover the lesions. Disseminated zoster, or any zoster in an immunocompromised client: airborne + contact precautions (negative-pressure room) until crusted, or until dissemination is ruled out. Antivirals work best within 72 hours. Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix, 2 doses) is recommended for adults ≥50 years. Postherpetic neuralgia is the major complication.
Herpes simplex (cold sores, genital herpes): grouped vesicles on a red base. Diagnose with PCR or Tzanck smear.
Warts (HPV) are common in children and adolescents. Some HPV types raise cancer risk (cervical, anal, oropharyngeal), so encourage HPV vaccination.

sections.heading: Fungal
sections.body: Dermatophytes (tinea) cause ring-shaped scaly patches with central clearing. Tinea pedis (athlete's foot), corporis (ringworm), cruris (jock itch), and capitis (scalp) are the common forms. Tinea capitis needs oral antifungals (griseofulvin or terbinafine for weeks), because topical agents don't reach the hair follicle. Candida thrives in warm, moist skin folds, especially in obesity, diabetes, and antibiotic use. Diagnose with a KOH prep. Teach the client to dry skin folds and between the toes thoroughly, wear cotton socks and shower shoes, and not share combs or hats. Fungal infections are more dangerous in immunocompromised clients.

sections.heading: Parasitic
bullets: Pediculosis (lice): nits cemented to hair shafts near the scalp, with itching. Use permethrin 1% or another pediculicide per label. Don't use conditioner or combination shampoo-conditioner before treatment. Comb out nits with a fine-tooth nit comb. Wash bedding, clothing, and hats in hot water (≥130°F / 54°C) and dry on high heat, or seal non-washables in a plastic bag for 2 weeks. Soak combs and brushes in hot water. Don't share hats or combs. Fumigant sprays are not recommended. The AAP advises that children can return to school after treatment, so “no-nit” policies are discouraged.

Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei mite): intense itching that is worse at night, and linear burrows in the finger webs, wrists, waistline, and genitals. Apply permethrin 5% to clean, cool, dry skin from the neck to the soles, including between the fingers and toes and under the nails. Leave it on 8–14 hours, wash it off, and repeat in about 1 week. Treat all household and close contacts at the same time. Wash bedding and clothing from the previous 3 days in hot water, or bag them for at least 72 hours. Itching may continue for 2–4 weeks after successful treatment. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies in debilitated clients is highly contagious and needs contact precautions.

pearls: Varicella and disseminated zoster: airborne + contact until ALL lesions are crusted. Healthcare workers who are not immune and pregnant staff should not be assigned to these clients.
Mark the cellulitis border with a pen at first assessment. Spread beyond the line is objective evidence that therapy is failing.
Scabies = treat everyone in the household at once. Lice = treat only those who are infested, and check everyone.
Children with chickenpox should never get aspirin (Reye syndrome). Use acetaminophen for fever.
redFlags: Cellulitis with rapid spread, severe pain, crepitus, bullae, or signs of sepsis (possible necrotizing fasciitis)
Zoster involving the tip of the nose or the eye (ophthalmic branch). It threatens vision, so refer urgently.
Dark urine, periorbital edema, or hypertension 1–3 weeks after strep impetigo (glomerulonephritis)

topics.title: Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
topics.summary: Dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, and acne are chronic, itchy, visible conditions. They affect comfort, sleep, and self-image.

sections.heading: Contact dermatitis
bullets: Irritant contact dermatitis is the most common type. It is direct, non-immune chemical damage from soaps, detergents, solvents, frequent hand washing, or urine and stool (diaper dermatitis). Redness, dryness, cracking, and burning are limited to the exposed area. It can happen on first exposure, and infants have the strongest irritant response.

Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV (delayed, T-cell) hypersensitivity that needs prior sensitization. The rash appears 24–72 hours after re-exposure, exactly in the shape of the contact (a watchband, a jeans snap from nickel, linear streaks from poison ivy), with itching, vesicles, and wheals. Adults have most allergic cases, and older adults react more slowly and less intensely. Diagnose with patch testing.

Treatment: identify and avoid the trigger, use cool compresses, emollients, topical corticosteroids, and oral antihistamines for itching, and give systemic steroids for severe or widespread poison ivy.

sections.heading: Latex allergy
sections.body: Healthcare workers, clients with spina bifida, and anyone who has had many surgeries or catheterizations are at risk. Reactions range from irritant dermatitis to type IV contact dermatitis to type I IgE-mediated anaphylaxis. Latex-fruit syndrome is cross-reactivity with banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut, so ask about these foods. Management: latex-free environment and supplies (gloves, catheters, BP cuffs, tourniquets), allergy band and signage, schedule surgery as the first case of the day when possible, and a medical-alert ID and epinephrine auto-injector if the client has had a systemic reaction.

sections.heading: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
sections.body: A chronic, relapsing, intensely itchy inflammation caused by a defective skin barrier. It is part of the atopic triad (eczema, allergic rhinitis, asthma). Infants get it on the cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces. Older children and adults get it in the flexural creases (antecubital, popliteal). In darker skin it may look violaceous or gray-brown rather than red, and follicular papules are common. Care: short lukewarm baths, mild fragrance-free cleanser, pat dry and apply a thick emollient within 3 minutes (“soak and seal”), cotton clothing, short nails, avoid triggers (wool, fragrance, heat, stress), and topical steroids or calcineurin inhibitors for flares. Scratching invites secondary infection with staph or herpes (eczema herpeticum).

sections.heading: Psoriasis
sections.body: A chronic, immune-mediated disorder in which the epidermis turns over far too fast (days instead of about a month). It forms well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scale on the elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back, sometimes with nail pitting. In darker skin, plaques may look violet or dark brown with gray scale. It is associated with psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular disease, and depression. Trauma to skin can trigger new plaques (Koebner phenomenon). Triggers include stress, infection (strep), injury, cold dry weather, alcohol, smoking, and some drugs (beta blockers, lithium). Treatment includes topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs (calcipotriene), coal tar, phototherapy (UVB), methotrexate, and biologics. Screen for TB and infection before starting biologics, and give no live vaccines while on them.

sections.heading: Acne vulgaris
sections.body: Puberty hormones (androgens) increase sebum. Clogged follicles plus Cutibacterium acnes lead to comedones, papules, pustules, and cysts. It affects about 85% of people aged 12–24. Teach: wash gently twice daily, don't pick or squeeze, use non-comedogenic products, and expect topical treatments to take 6–8 weeks. Darker skin is prone to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and keloid scarring, so treat early.

table.caption: Irritant vs allergic contact dermatitis
rows: Diffuse at exposed area; dry, cracked, burning
Sharply outlines the allergen shape; itchy vesicles/wheals
Nickel, poison ivy, latex, fragrance, dyes

pearls: A rash that exactly matches the shape of a watch, ring, or jeans button suggests allergic contact dermatitis (nickel).
Latex allergy: always ask about banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut reactions.
Eczema: “soak and seal.” Take lukewarm baths and apply emollient within 3 minutes of patting dry.
Before any biologic for psoriasis or eczema: TB screen, check vaccine status, no live vaccines.
redFlags: Wheezing, stridor, hypotension, or generalized urticaria after latex exposure means anaphylaxis. Give epinephrine IM.
Punched-out vesicles or erosions with fever in a child with eczema (eczema herpeticum). This is an emergency.

topics.title: Skin Cancer & Sun Protection
topics.summary: Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the U.S. Most of it is preventable, and it is highly curable when caught early.

sections.heading: Types of skin cancer
bullets: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type. It is a pearly or waxy papule with rolled borders and telangiectasia, sometimes with a central ulcer, on sun-exposed skin. It grows slowly and rarely metastasizes but is locally destructive.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a rough, scaly, crusted or ulcerated nodule. Actinic keratosis is the precancerous lesion. SCC can metastasize, especially on the lips, ears, or in chronic wounds and scars.

Malignant melanoma is the most serious and deadly type. It arises from melanocytes, metastasizes early, and can appear anywhere. Risk factors: fair skin, blistering sunburns (especially in childhood), tanning beds, many or atypical moles, family history, and immunosuppression. In people with darker skin, acral lentiginous melanoma appears on the palms, soles, and nail beds (a dark streak under the nail), and it is often diagnosed late.

sections.heading: ABCDE warning signs of melanoma
bullets: Asymmetry: one half doesn't match the other
Border: irregular, notched, or blurred
Color: varied shades of brown, black, red, white, or blue
Diameter: >6 mm (about a pencil eraser), though melanomas can be smaller
Evolving: any change in size, shape, color, or elevation, or new bleeding, itching, or crusting
Also: the “ugly duckling” sign, a mole that looks different from the client's other moles

sections.heading: Sun protection teaching
bullets: Use a broad-spectrum (UVA + UVB), water-resistant sunscreen with SPF ≥30 every day, including on cloudy days. SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB.
Apply about 1 oz (a shot glass) for the whole body 15 minutes before going out. Reapply every 2 hours, and right after swimming or sweating (“water resistant” lasts 40 or 80 minutes).
Seek shade from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.. Wear a wide-brimmed hat, UV-blocking sunglasses, and protective clothing (UPF).
Avoid tanning beds. There is no such thing as a “safe base tan.”
Infants <6 months: keep out of direct sun and use shade and clothing. Sunscreen can be applied to small exposed areas if shade isn't available.
Photosensitizing drugs increase burn risk: tetracyclines (doxycycline), sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones, thiazides, isotretinoin, amiodarone, some chemotherapy.
Clients of all skin tones need sun protection. Darker skin burns less easily but still gets skin cancer and melasma.

pearls: Melanoma is the most serious, and BCC is the most common. SCC is in between (can metastasize; actinic keratosis is the precursor).
In darker skin, teach inspection of the palms, soles, and nail beds. A new dark streak in a nail needs evaluation.
Benign lesions to recognize: seborrheic keratosis (“stuck-on,” waxy, older adults), cherry angiomas, and skin tags. These don't need urgent referral unless they change.
redFlags: Any mole that is changing (evolving) or bleeding, or that meets ABCDE criteria. Refer for biopsy.
A non-healing sore or ulcer in a scar or chronic wound (possible SCC).

topics.title: Wound Types & Classification
topics.summary: Classifying a wound by cause, skin integrity, contamination, and depth predicts infection risk and shapes the plan.

sections.heading: By cause and skin integrity
bullets: Intentional wounds are made for therapy: surgical incisions, venipuncture, IV or drain sites. They are created under aseptic conditions with clean edges.
Unintentional wounds are accidental: lacerations, abrasions, punctures, gunshot wounds, bites, open fractures. They are contaminated from the start.
Closed wounds: the skin is intact but underlying tissue is injured (contusion/bruise, hematoma, sprain, closed fracture).
Open wounds: the skin or mucous membrane is broken (abrasion, laceration, puncture, incision). This is a portal of entry for microorganisms.

sections.heading: CDC surgical wound classification (by contamination)
bullets: Class I – Clean: an uninfected operative wound with no inflammation, where the respiratory, alimentary (GI), genital, or urinary tract is not entered. Example: thyroidectomy, hernia repair, joint replacement.

Class II – Clean-contaminated: the respiratory, GI, genital, or urinary tract is entered under controlled conditions without unusual contamination. Example: elective cholecystectomy, non-inflamed appendectomy, hysterectomy, elective colon resection with prepped bowel.

Class III – Contaminated: open, fresh, accidental wounds, a major break in sterile technique, gross spillage from the GI tract, or acute non-purulent inflammation. Example: fresh laceration, spillage during bowel surgery.

Class IV – Dirty/Infected: old traumatic wounds with devitalized tissue, existing clinical infection (pus), or perforated viscera. Example: ruptured appendix with abscess, draining wound abscess. The organisms were in the field before surgery.

sections.heading: By depth
bullets: Partial-thickness: loss of the epidermis and possibly part of the dermis. Dermal appendages (hair follicles, glands) remain, so it heals by regeneration, fairly quickly, with little or no scarring. It is often painful because nerve endings are exposed.

Full-thickness: loss of the epidermis and all of the dermis, possibly extending into subcutaneous tissue, muscle, or bone. It heals by connective tissue (scar) repair, slowly, and may need grafting or flaps.

sections.heading: Acute wound care (untreated wounds)
bullets: Control bleeding: use standard precautions, then apply firm direct pressure with a sterile or clean dressing and elevate above the heart. Don't remove an impaled object. Stabilize it instead.

Prevent infection: once bleeding is controlled, irrigate and clean with normal saline or potable water, then cover with a sterile dressing. Check tetanus status: a booster is needed if >5 years for dirty or major wounds, or >10 years for clean minor wounds.
Reduce pain and swelling: apply ice (wrapped, 15–20 minutes) to closed wounds and contusions.
Assess for shock: rapid weak pulse, cool clammy skin, hypotension, restlessness.
Treated wounds: at each dressing change, assess for healing, drainage, pain, and signs of infection.

table.caption: CDC wound class and infection risk
rows: Fresh accidental wound, sterile break, GI spillage
Existing infection, pus, perforation, old devitalized tissue

pearls: Tract entered on purpose and under control = clean-contaminated. Spillage or a fresh accident = contaminated. Pus or perforation already there = dirty.
Pressure first, elevation second. Irrigation and dressing come only after bleeding is controlled.
Partial-thickness wounds regenerate. Full-thickness wounds scar.
redFlags: Bleeding that soaks through dressings despite direct pressure, or signs of hypovolemic shock
Any wound with pus, perforation, or devitalized tissue (Class IV). Anticipate antibiotics and debridement.

topics.title: Diagnostics, Labs & Nutrition
topics.summary: The right test identifies the cause, and the right labs and nutrition show whether tissue can heal.

sections.heading: Diagnostic tests
bullets: Skin biopsy (punch, shave, excisional) is the definitive test for benign vs malignant lesions. Afterward: keep the site clean, watch for bleeding, and teach suture care.

Cultures and sensitivity of tissue, drainage, or exudate identify the organism and guide antibiotics. Collect them before starting antibiotics. For wounds, clean with saline first, then culture viable tissue (Levine technique), not pus or old exudate.
KOH (potassium hydroxide) prep: scrapings are dissolved to show fungal hyphae and spores (tinea, candida).
Wood lamp: UV (black light) exam in a darkened room. Some tinea capitis fluoresces blue-green, erythrasma coral-red, and vitiligo shows as sharply bright white depigmentation.
Tzanck smear: scrapings from the base of a vesicle show multinucleated giant cells (herpes simplex, varicella-zoster). PCR is now more specific.
Immunofluorescence studies detect antibodies in autoimmune blistering disease (pemphigus) and lupus.

Allergy testing: scratch/prick and intradermal tests detect type I (IgE) allergy, and patch testing detects type IV contact allergy. Patches stay on and dry for 48 hours, with readings at 48 and about 72–96 hours. Hold antihistamines before prick/intradermal testing, and have emergency equipment ready.
Carrier studies: nasal cultures for S. aureus/MRSA in clients with recurrent infections.

sections.heading: Labs that affect healing
bullets: WBC: ↓ = poor defense against infection and delayed healing. ↑ may signal infection.
Hemoglobin/hematocrit: ↓ = less oxygen delivered to tissue.
Coagulation (PT/INR, aPTT, platelets): prolonged times → bleeding and hematoma. Hypercoagulability → clotting and poor perfusion.

Albumin (normal 3.5–5.0 g/dL): <3.5 g/dL = poor protein status, ↑ infection risk, and delayed healing. Its half-life is about 20 days, so it changes slowly, and inflammation and fluid status also affect it.
Prealbumin (about 15–36 mg/dL): its half-life is 2–3 days, so it reflects recent nutritional changes and response to supplements. <15 mg/dL suggests protein malnutrition.
Blood glucose / HbA1c: hyperglycemia impairs neutrophils and collagen synthesis and slows healing.
Wound cultures confirm infection and guide antibiotic choice.

sections.heading: Nutrition for tissue integrity
sections.body: Healing tissue needs extra calories and protein (often about 30–35 kcal/kg and 1.25–1.5 g protein/kg/day for clients with wounds, unless renal disease limits this), plus vitamin C (collagen synthesis), vitamin A (epithelialization, and it counters the effects of steroids), zinc (cell proliferation), and adequate fluids. Encourage lean proteins, dairy, eggs, whole grains, vegetables, and citrus. Offer small frequent meals or oral supplements when intake is poor, and consult the dietitian.

sections.heading: Independent nursing interventions
bullets: Goals: control the disease, prevent infection, promote healing, and relieve itching and pain.
Ask about home remedies and over-the-counter products, which may irritate the skin or delay healing.

Hygiene: daily bathing for most adults. Every other day, or as needed, is often enough for young children and older adults. Use lukewarm water and mild or liquid non-soap cleansers, pat dry, and moisturize right after bathing.

Infection prevention: hand hygiene before and after wound care, clean technique for dressings, safe disposal of soiled dressings, and teaching signs of infection (↑ redness, warmth, swelling, purulent drainage, odor, fever, necrosis).
Exercise and repositioning promote blood flow. Collaborate with wound care nurses, dietitians, dermatologists, surgeons, and case managers.

pearls: Albumin <3.5 g/dL = delayed healing risk. Prealbumin is the better marker of recent changes because of its 2–3 day half-life.
Get the culture before the first antibiotic dose.
KOH = fungus. Tzanck = herpes viruses. Patch test = contact (type IV) allergy. Biopsy = cancer.
redFlags: A wound client with albumin <3.5 g/dL, poor intake, and weight loss needs a dietitian referral and a nutrition plan now.
Fever, spreading redness, purulent drainage, or new odor from a wound

topics.title: Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
topics.summary: Most skin drugs are topical. That doesn't make them harmless, and one (isotretinoin) is among the most teratogenic drugs in use.

sections.heading: Acne medications
bullets: Benzoyl peroxide (OTC, first-line) is antibacterial against C. acnes and mildly comedolytic. Start with a low strength (2.5–5%) once daily. It causes dryness and peeling and bleaches hair, towels, and clothing. Use sunscreen.
Salicylic acid (OTC) exfoliates (keratolytic) and reduces inflammation. It is also used for warts. Avoid large areas and use in young children (salicylate toxicity).
Topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene) unplug follicles. They cause photosensitivity, so apply at night.

Isotretinoin (oral) is for severe nodular or cystic acne. It is highly teratogenic and dispensed only through the iPLEDGE REMS program. Clients who can become pregnant must commit to two forms of contraception (or abstinence) starting 1 month before therapy, during therapy, and for 1 month after the last dose, with pregnancy testing before and throughout. Other teaching: no blood donation during therapy or for 1 month after, no sharing pills, no vitamin A supplements, avoid alcohol. Monitor lipids and liver enzymes. Report mood changes or suicidal thoughts, severe headache or visual changes (intracranial hypertension), and abdominal pain. Expect dry skin, lips, and eyes, and photosensitivity.

sections.heading: Topical corticosteroids
sections.body: Used for eczema, psoriasis, and dermatitis. Potency ranges from low (hydrocortisone 1%) to super-high (clobetasol). Apply a thin layer to clean, slightly damp skin, rubbing in gently in the direction of hair growth. Use gloves or wash hands afterward. Avoid high-potency products on the face, groin, axillae, and skin folds. Don't cover with occlusive dressings or tight diapers unless prescribed, because this increases absorption. Taper long courses. Adverse effects include skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, and delayed healing. Infants and young children have a high surface-area-to-weight ratio, so systemic absorption can cause adrenal suppression.

sections.heading: Other agents
bullets: Pediculicides / scabicides: permethrin 1% (lice) and 5% (scabies). Oral ivermectin for resistant cases.
Antifungals: topical azoles or terbinafine. Oral terbinafine or griseofulvin for tinea capitis and nails (monitor LFTs).
Antivirals: acyclovir or valacyclovir for HSV and zoster. Start early and keep the client hydrated.
Antibiotics: topical mupirocin (impetigo). Oral agents for cellulitis. Some cause photosensitivity (doxycycline, sulfonamides).
Antihistamines for itching. Sedating first-generation drugs (diphenhydramine) are a fall risk in older adults.
Systemic immunomodulators (methotrexate, biologics) for severe psoriasis or eczema: infection risk, TB screening, no live vaccines. Methotrexate is teratogenic and hepatotoxic.

sections.heading: Nonpharmacologic, complementary, and team care
sections.body: Nonpharmacologic care includes proper wound care and dressing changes, nutrition, and specialized treatments such as daily debridement and sterile dressings for burns and negative-pressure wound therapy (a wound vac) for severe wounds. Complementary products such as aloe vera, chamomile, and evening primrose oil may soothe irritation, but evidence is limited. Ask about them and watch for allergy (chamomile cross-reacts with ragweed) and drug interactions. Darker skin is more prone to post-inflammatory pigment change, so combination therapy (chemical peels, microdermabrasion) may be used cautiously. The interprofessional team includes nurses, UAPs, wound care nurses, dietitians, case managers, dermatologists, oncologists, and surgeons. Good communication means fewer complications.

pearls: Isotretinoin: two forms of contraception, 1 month before, during, and 1 month after. No blood donation. Report depression.
Topical steroid: a thin layer only. No occlusion unless ordered, and no high-potency products on the face or groin.
Benzoyl peroxide bleaches fabric. Tell the client to use white towels and pillowcases.
redFlags: A client on isotretinoin who reports a missed period, a positive pregnancy test, depression, or suicidal thoughts. Stop the drug and notify the provider now.
Fever or new infection in a client on biologics or methotrexate

topics.title: Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Newborn, adolescent, pregnant, and aging skin each have expected findings. The nurse must know which ones are normal and which are warning signs.

sections.heading: Newborns and infants
bullets: Vernix caseosa is a white, cheesy coating that protects the skin and helps regulate temperature. It doesn't need to be scrubbed off.
Thin skin, a large surface area, and little subcutaneous fat mean greater heat loss and greater absorption of topical agents. Use products sparingly and avoid adult products.

Expected findings: milia (white papules on the nose and chin from blocked sebaceous glands), erythema toxicum (blotchy red macules with white or yellow central papules that appear at 24–72 hours, come and go, and resolve on their own), neonatal acne, acrocyanosis in the first 24–48 hours, lanugo, desquamation in post-term infants, and stork bites (nevus simplex).

Congenital dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots): blue-gray patches over the sacrum and buttocks, common in darker-skinned infants. Document them at birth so they aren't mistaken for bruising or abuse.
Birthmarks to report: port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) on the face in the trigeminal area (possible Sturge-Weber syndrome), and large or rapidly growing hemangiomas near the eyes or airway.
Unexpected: jaundice in the first 24 hours (pathologic), widespread petechiae, and central cyanosis.

sections.heading: Children and adolescents
sections.body: Children have a larger body surface area (↑ fluid and heat loss) and frequent infections: tinea, warts, varicella, impetigo, lice, and scabies. Other childhood rashes include fifth disease (“slapped cheek”), roseola (a rash that appears after 3 days of high fever), and pityriasis rosea (a herald patch, then a “Christmas tree” pattern). Diaper dermatitis prevention: frequent changes, air-drying, and zinc oxide barrier cream. In adolescents, puberty hormones ↑ sebum and sweating, which leads to acne, dermatitis, psoriasis flares, fungal infections, and warts. Acne strongly affects body image, so address it with psychosocial support as well as treatment.

sections.heading: Pregnancy
sections.body: Hormonal changes cause hyperpigmentation: linea nigra, melasma/chloasma (the “mask of pregnancy”), and darkened areolae. Others include striae gravidarum (stretch marks), spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and pruritus. Atopic eruption of pregnancy is the most common pregnancy dermatosis: an eczematous, itchy rash that usually starts early and resolves postpartum. Red flag: intense itching of the palms and soles, usually worse at night, in the third trimester without a primary rash suggests intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Report it, because it needs serum bile acids and LFTs and carries a risk of stillbirth.

sections.heading: Older adults
bullets: Intrinsic aging starts at about age 20: slower cell turnover, ↓ moisture and fat. Collagen falls in the 40s, causing wrinkles. After menopause, less estrogen means thinner, drier skin. Extrinsic aging comes from UV, smoking, pollution, and chemicals, causing thickening, precancerous changes, and deep wrinkles.

Expected changes: thin, less elastic, translucent, paler skin (fewer melanocytes); dry, itchy skin (xerosis) from ↓ sebaceous activity; ↓ subcutaneous fat (less cushioning, poor thermoregulation); ↓ sensation; slower healing; senile purpura from fragile vessels; age spots (lentigines); seborrheic keratoses; cherry angiomas.

Nursing implications: high risk of skin tears, pressure injury, burns (↓ sensation), and hypothermia. Bathe every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser, pat dry, and moisturize while the skin is still damp. Lift with a draw sheet rather than dragging. Pad bed rails and wheelchair arms. Use silicone or paper tape (or none) and long sleeves for protection. Ensure fluids and nutrition.

pearls: Erythema toxicum is benign and self-limiting. Reassure the parents and don't treat it.
Document Mongolian spots at birth. They are not bruises.
Itching of the palms and soles in the 3rd trimester with no rash suggests cholestasis. Report it.
Older adults: no hot water, no vigorous rubbing, no adhesive tape on fragile skin, and never drag the client up in bed.
redFlags: Jaundice appearing within 24 hours of birth
Petechiae or bruising in patterns that don't match the history, in any age group (possible abuse or bleeding disorder)

flashcards.front: Which skin layer contains blood vessels, nerve endings, and sweat and sebaceous glands?
flashcards.back: The dermis, the “working layer.” The epidermis is avascular.

flashcards.front: Name five functions of the skin.
flashcards.back: Protection, sensation, thermoregulation, excretion (sweat), vitamin D synthesis. It also maintains fluid balance and supports immunity.

flashcards.front: What does the subcutaneous tissue do?
flashcards.back: It stores about half of the body's fat, insulates, cushions, and anchors skin to underlying structures. Loss in older adults ↑ hypothermia and pressure risk.

flashcards.front: Where do you assess cyanosis in a client with dark skin?
flashcards.back: Oral (buccal) mucosa, lips, nail beds, conjunctivae. They may look ashen gray.

flashcards.front: How do you detect inflammation or early pressure damage in darker skin?
flashcards.back: Palpate for warmth, induration, edema, or bogginess. Look for darker, taut, or shiny areas. Compare with adjacent skin and use natural light.

flashcards.front: Macule vs patch? Papule vs plaque? Vesicle vs bulla?
flashcards.back: Same lesion type, different size. Each pair splits at 1 cm: <1 cm = macule, papule, vesicle; >1 cm = patch, plaque, bulla.

flashcards.front: Primary vs secondary lesion?
flashcards.back: Primary arises from normal skin (macule, papule, nodule, vesicle, pustule, bulla, wheal). Secondary evolves from a primary lesion or trauma (crust, scale, scar, keloid, fissure, erosion, ulcer).

flashcards.front: Honey-colored crusts around a child's nose and mouth?
flashcards.back: Impetigo (staph or strep). Contact precautions, wash crusts off gently, mupirocin, stay out of school until 24 hours on antibiotics.

flashcards.front: Isolation for varicella or disseminated zoster?
flashcards.back: Airborne + contact (negative-pressure room) until all lesions are crusted. Localized zoster in an immunocompetent client: standard precautions with lesions covered.

flashcards.front: Key teaching for scabies treatment?
flashcards.back: Permethrin 5% from the neck to the soles, left on 8–14 hours, repeated in about 1 week. Treat all close contacts at the same time. Hot-wash linens or bag them for 72 hours. Itching may last 2–4 weeks.

flashcards.front: First nursing action when cellulitis is diagnosed on the lower leg?
flashcards.back: Outline the border of redness with a skin marker (date and time) to track spread. Also elevate the leg, give antibiotics, and monitor temperature and WBC.

flashcards.front: Irritant vs allergic contact dermatitis?
flashcards.back: Irritant: non-immune chemical damage that can occur on first exposure. Allergic: type IV delayed hypersensitivity, 24–72 hours after re-exposure, shaped like the allergen. Diagnosed by patch test.

flashcards.front: Foods that cross-react with latex?
flashcards.back: Banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut (latex-fruit syndrome).

flashcards.front: Classic psoriasis lesion?
flashcards.back: Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery-white scale on the elbows, knees, and scalp. Nail pitting. Koebner phenomenon.

flashcards.front: “Soak and seal” for eczema?
flashcards.back: Short lukewarm bath, pat dry, and apply a thick emollient within 3 minutes to lock in moisture.

flashcards.front: ABCDE of melanoma?
flashcards.back: Asymmetry, Border irregular, Color variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving.

flashcards.front: Most common skin cancer? Most deadly?
flashcards.back: Most common: basal cell carcinoma (rarely metastasizes). Most deadly: malignant melanoma.

flashcards.front: Sunscreen teaching essentials?
flashcards.back: Broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF ≥30. Apply 15 minutes before going out, reapply every 2 hours and after swimming or sweating. Avoid sun from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and avoid tanning beds.

flashcards.front: Where does melanoma often appear in people with darker skin?
flashcards.back: Palms, soles, and nail beds (acral lentiginous melanoma), often as a new dark streak under a nail.

flashcards.front: The 4 CDC surgical wound classes?
flashcards.back: I Clean (no tract entered), II Clean-contaminated (tract entered under control), III Contaminated (fresh accidental wound, sterile break, spillage), IV Dirty/Infected (pus, perforation, old devitalized tissue).

flashcards.front: Closed vs open wound?
flashcards.back: Closed: skin intact, underlying tissue injured (contusion). Open: skin or mucous membrane broken (laceration, incision).

flashcards.front: Partial vs full-thickness healing?
flashcards.back: Partial (epidermis ± part of dermis) heals by regeneration. Full (all skin layers ± deeper) heals by connective tissue / scar repair.

flashcards.front: First-aid priorities for a bleeding laceration?
flashcards.back: Gloves → direct pressure → elevate → irrigate with saline once bleeding is controlled → sterile dressing. Assess for shock and check tetanus status.

flashcards.front: Albumin value that signals risk for delayed healing?
flashcards.back: <3.5 g/dL. Prealbumin (half-life 2–3 days) better reflects recent nutritional change.

flashcards.front: KOH prep, Wood lamp, Tzanck smear: what does each detect?
flashcards.back: KOH: fungal hyphae. Wood lamp: UV fluorescence (some tinea, vitiligo, erythrasma). Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells (HSV/VZV).

flashcards.front: Nutrients that support tissue repair?
flashcards.back: ↑ Calories and protein, vitamin C (collagen), vitamin A (epithelialization), zinc, and adequate fluids.

flashcards.front: Isotretinoin: key safety requirement?
flashcards.back: iPLEDGE REMS: 2 forms of contraception from 1 month before until 1 month after therapy, pregnancy testing, no blood donation. Report mood changes.

flashcards.front: How to apply a topical corticosteroid?
flashcards.back: Thin layer, no occlusion unless ordered, avoid high potency on the face and groin, taper long courses. Watch for atrophy and striae, and for systemic absorption in children.

flashcards.front: Erythema toxicum?
flashcards.back: A benign newborn rash of red blotches with white or yellow papules, appearing at 24–72 hours and resolving on its own. No treatment.

flashcards.front: Why bathe older adults every other day with lukewarm water?
flashcards.back: ↓ Sebaceous glands → dry, fragile skin. Frequent hot bathing strips oils → xerosis, itching, and skin tears.

questions.hintContent: Recall which skin layer is avascular and which layer holds the blood vessels and nerve endings.
questions.hintStrategy: Two cues in the stem, bleeding and pain, each point to a structure. Find the only layer that contains both.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Layers of the Skin
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client has a superficial abrasion that is oozing small amounts of blood and is painful to touch. The nurse recognizes that the injury has reached which skin layer?
options: The stratum corneum of the epidermis only
The dermis, which contains blood vessels and nerve endings
The subcutaneous layer, which stores adipose tissue
The basal layer of the epidermis, which contains capillaries
optionRationales: The stratum corneum is dead keratinized cells with no vessels or nerves, so injury limited to it would not bleed or hurt.
Correct. The epidermis is avascular. Bleeding and pain mean the injury has reached the dermis, where the blood vessels and sensory nerve endings are.
The subcutaneous layer is fat and connective tissue. A superficial abrasion does not usually reach it.
The basal layer has no capillaries. The epidermis is nourished by diffusion from the dermis.
questions.rationale: The epidermis contains no blood vessels. Any wound that bleeds has reached at least the dermis, the “working layer” that holds vessels, nerves, glands, and hair follicles.
questions.takeaway: If it bleeds, it has reached the dermis.

questions.hintContent: Think about what intact skin prevents minute to minute: microbial entry and evaporative water and heat loss.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a priority item. Rank options by Maslow and ABCs. Physiological threats to circulation outrank psychosocial or long-term concerns.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Functions of the Skin
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client is admitted after losing a large area of epidermis and dermis over the back and legs. Based on the normal functions of the skin, which nursing problem is the priority?
options: Impaired vitamin D synthesis from reduced UV absorption in the damaged skin
Disturbed body image related to visible skin loss on the back and legs
Decreased tactile sensation and pain perception over the affected areas
Fluid volume deficit and infection from loss of the protective barrier
optionRationales: Vitamin D synthesis is a real skin function, but losing it is not an immediate threat to life.
Body image matters, but psychosocial needs come after physiological threats.
Loss of sensation is a safety concern, but it is less urgent than fluid loss and infection.
Correct. The skin is the barrier against microorganisms and evaporative water loss. Large skin loss quickly leads to hypovolemia, hypothermia, and sepsis, which threaten circulation and life.
questions.rationale: Protection (from infection and fluid loss) and thermoregulation are the skin functions whose loss threatens life. Maslow and ABC priorities place physiological threats, especially circulation and fluid volume, above psychosocial and long-term concerns.
questions.takeaway: Large skin loss = fluid loss + infection + heat loss. These are the immediate threats.

questions.hintContent: Recall where melanocytes, nerve endings, sebaceous glands, and fat stores are located, and what each one does.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row, name the function that is failing first (insulation? sensation? oil? pigment? cushioning?), then match that function to its layer.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Layers of the Skin
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An 84-year-old client in a long-term care facility has the following findings. For each finding, identify the skin layer whose age-related change best explains it.
rows: Reports feeling cold in a 72°F (22°C) room and needs extra blankets
Did not notice a burn from a heating pad left on the lower back
Has very dry, flaky, itchy skin on the shins
Skin appears paler and more translucent than in earlier photos
Has little cushioning over the sacrum and heels
optionRationales: Subcutaneous tissue. Loss of subcutaneous fat reduces insulation, so older adults lose heat easily and are at risk for hypothermia.
Dermis. Sensory nerve endings sit in the dermis. Reduced sensation with aging raises the risk of burns and injury.
Dermis. Sebaceous and sweat glands live in the dermis. Reduced sebum causes xerosis (dry, itchy skin).
Epidermis. Melanocytes sit in the basal epidermis. Fewer melanocytes with aging cause paler, translucent skin and less UV protection.
Subcutaneous tissue. The hypodermis cushions bony prominences. Its loss increases pressure injury risk.
questions.rationale: Relating findings to structure lets the nurse predict risk. The epidermis holds the melanocytes. The dermis holds the nerves and glands, so its changes cause reduced sensation and dry skin. Loss of subcutaneous fat reduces insulation and cushioning.
questions.takeaway: Aging skin: fewer melanocytes (epidermis), less sensation and oil (dermis), less fat (subcutaneous).

questions.hintContent: Color changes are easiest to see where melanin is sparse.
questions.hintStrategy: Central cyanosis reflects oxygenation of arterial blood. Choose a site that is both central and minimally pigmented.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Cultural Considerations in Skin Assessment

questions.stem: A client with deeply pigmented skin and a COPD exacerbation has an SpO2 of 86% on 2 L/min nasal cannula and is increasingly short of breath. The nurse wants to assess for central cyanosis. Which area should the nurse inspect?
options: The skin of the forehead and cheeks
The oral mucosa and conjunctivae
The skin over the sternum
The dorsal surface of the hands
optionRationales: Heavily pigmented facial skin hides the bluish or gray tint of cyanosis.
Correct. The oral (buccal) mucosa, lips, conjunctivae, and nail beds have the least melanin, so cyanosis (often ashen gray in dark skin) is easiest to see there.
Sternal skin is useful for testing turgor in older adults but not for detecting cyanosis in dark skin.
The back of the hand is pigmented and shows peripheral, not central, changes.
questions.rationale: In darker skin, color changes are best seen where melanin is minimal: mucous membranes, conjunctivae, nail beds, palms, and soles. Central cyanosis is best judged in the mouth.
questions.takeaway: Dark skin: look where melanin is least, in the mucosa, conjunctivae, nail beds, palms, and soles.

questions.hintContent: Consider which assessment findings do not depend on seeing redness.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option on its own as true or false. Watch for options that rely on a visual cue that melanin can hide.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Cultural Considerations in Skin Assessment
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing the sacrum of a client with dark brown skin who has been on bed rest for 3 days. Which techniques will help the nurse detect early tissue damage? Select all that apply.
options: Palpate the area for warmth compared with surrounding skin
Check for induration, edema, or a boggy feel
Inspect for areas that look darker, taut, or shiny
Rely on the presence of blanchable redness
Assess the area under overhead fluorescent light only
Lightly moisten the skin to make color changes easier to see
optionRationales: Correct. Warmth (or coolness) compared with adjacent skin is an early sign of inflammation or tissue damage that doesn't depend on color.
Correct. Induration, edema, and bogginess are palpable changes that reveal damage melanin may hide.
Correct. In darker skin, inflammation often looks darker (purple or maroon), taut, shiny, or indurated rather than red.
Incorrect. Redness and blanching may be impossible to see in dark skin. Relying on them leads to missed injury.
Incorrect. Natural or halogen light is preferred. Fluorescent light can give skin a bluish cast and hide changes.
Correct. Slightly moistening the skin can make subtle color and sheen changes easier to see.
questions.rationale: Detecting erythema by eye is unreliable in darkly pigmented skin. The nurse compensates by palpating for temperature, induration, and edema, looking for darker, shiny, or taut areas, using good natural light, and comparing with adjacent skin.
questions.takeaway: In dark skin, feel for warmth and induration. Don't wait to see redness.

questions.hintContent: Review how pallor and cyanosis look in darkly pigmented skin and which sites show them best.
questions.hintStrategy: Look at the vital signs first. Then pick the skin finding that explains them, not the chronic or cosmetic findings.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Cultural Considerations in Skin Assessment
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: Four hours after abdominal surgery, a client with dark skin is restless. Vital signs: HR 122/min, BP 92/58 mm Hg, RR 24/min, SpO2 93%. Which assessment finding requires the most immediate follow-up?
options: Hyperpigmented macules on the forearms from a previous rash
Dry, flaking skin on both lower legs
Ashen-gray lips and pale conjunctivae
A 2-cm keloid on the right earlobe
optionRationales: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is common after healed lesions in darker skin and is not urgent.
Dry skin (xerosis) is a comfort and skin-care issue, not an acute threat.

Correct. Ashen-gray color and pale conjunctivae are how pallor and cyanosis look in dark skin. With tachycardia, hypotension, and restlessness after surgery, they suggest hemorrhage or hypovolemic shock and need immediate action.
Keloids are more common in darker skin and are a chronic cosmetic finding.
questions.rationale: In dark skin, pallor looks ashen gray (or yellow-brown), and changes are best seen in the lips, mucosa, and conjunctivae. With abnormal vital signs, this points to impaired perfusion, an ABC priority.
questions.takeaway: Ashen gray + tachycardia + hypotension in dark skin = shock until proven otherwise.

questions.hintContent: Primary lesions are named by what they contain (solid, clear fluid, pus) and by size, with a cut-off at 1 cm.
questions.hintStrategy: Use two cues from the stem, the fluid type and the measurement, to eliminate options.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse notes several raised lesions on a child's trunk that are filled with clear fluid and measure about 0.5 cm each. How should the nurse document these lesions?
options: Vesicles
Pustules
Bullae
Wheals
optionRationales: Correct. A vesicle is a circumscribed, elevated, clear-fluid-filled primary lesion less than 1 cm, as seen in varicella or herpes.
Pustules contain purulent (cloudy, yellow) fluid, not clear fluid.
Bullae are clear-fluid-filled lesions larger than 1 cm.
Wheals are transient, edematous, irregular raised areas without a fluid-filled cavity, such as hives.
questions.rationale: Primary lesions are named by content and size. Clear fluid <1 cm is a vesicle, and >1 cm is a bulla. Pus-filled lesions are pustules.
questions.takeaway: Vesicle <1 cm, bulla >1 cm, and pustule = pus.

questions.hintContent: Primary lesions arise from normal skin. Secondary lesions develop from a primary lesion or from trauma.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row ask: could this appear on previously healthy skin, or does something have to happen first (drying, cracking, rupture)?
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 9-year-old is seen in the clinic for several skin complaints, and the nurse documents the findings below. Classify each finding as a primary or secondary lesion.
rows: Flat, brown, nonpalpable freckle 4 mm in diameter
Dried honey-colored exudate over a lesion
Transient raised, itchy hive after a bee sting
Linear crack in the skin between the toes
Pus-filled raised lesion on the chin
optionRationales: Primary. A flat color change <1 cm is a macule, arising from normal skin.
Secondary. A crust is dried serum, blood, or pus left after a primary lesion (such as an impetigo vesicle or pustule) ruptures.
Primary. A wheal arises directly from normal skin.
Secondary. A fissure is a crack that develops in skin changed by dryness or disease (for example, tinea pedis).
Primary. A pustule arises from previously normal skin.
questions.rationale: Primary lesions (macule, papule, nodule, vesicle, bulla, pustule, wheal) arise from previously normal skin. Secondary lesions (crust, scale, fissure, erosion, ulcer, scar, keloid) come from changes in primary lesions or from trauma.
questions.takeaway: Primary = the first lesion. Secondary = what it becomes (crust, scale, fissure, ulcer, scar).

questions.hintContent: Skin, hair, and nails can reflect endocrine disease. Consider which hormone controls metabolic rate and heat production.
questions.hintStrategy: Group all the cues, not just the skin ones. Cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and bradycardia point to one system. Then pick the test for that system.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin as a Reflection of Systemic Disease
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client reports dry, rough skin that lotions don't help, thinning hair, brittle nails, weight gain, constipation, and always feeling cold. HR 56/min. Complete the statement.
questions.template: The skin and hair findings most likely reflect {0}. The nurse should anticipate that the provider will order {1}.

options: hypothyroidism
contact dermatitis
psoriasis
iron-deficiency anemia
a KOH preparation of skin scrapings
a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level
a patch test
a Wood lamp examination

questions.rationale: Skin can mirror systemic disease. Dry, coarse skin, hair loss, and brittle nails with cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and bradycardia are classic signs of hypothyroidism. A TSH level is the first screening test. Dermatologic tests (KOH, patch, Wood lamp) look for local skin disease and would miss the cause.
questions.takeaway: Dry skin + hair loss + cold intolerance → think thyroid, not lotion.

questions.hintContent: Recall how impetigo spreads and the usual return-to-school rule after antibiotics start.
questions.hintStrategy: You are looking for the statement that shows CORRECT understanding. Eliminate any statement that would spread the infection or harm the skin.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A 5-year-old has honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth and is prescribed mupirocin ointment. Which statement by the parent indicates the teaching was effective?
options: “I'll gently wash the crusts off with soap and water before applying the ointment.”
“My child can go back to kindergarten tomorrow since the rash isn't itchy.”
“The whole family can keep sharing bath towels as long as we wash them weekly.”
“I'll cover the sores tightly with plastic wrap overnight so they heal faster.”
optionRationales: Correct. Gently removing the crusts with soap and water lets the topical antibiotic reach the bacteria and reduces the bacterial load.
Impetigo is highly contagious. The child should stay home until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics, whether or not the rash itches.
Towels, washcloths, and linens should not be shared. They spread staph and strep.
Occlusive plastic wrap traps moisture and is not part of impetigo care. It can worsen maceration and spread.
questions.rationale: Impetigo (S. aureus or group A strep) spreads by direct contact. Care: gently remove crusts, apply the prescribed antibiotic, keep nails short, don't share personal items, wash hands, and exclude from school or daycare until 24 hours of therapy.
questions.takeaway: Impetigo: remove crusts, apply mupirocin, share nothing, stay home until 24 hours on antibiotics.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A 22-year-old client with recurrent herpes simplex labialis (cold sores) is prescribed valacyclovir to take at the start of each outbreak. Which instructions should the nurse include in the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Take the first dose at the earliest tingling or burning, before blisters form
Avoid kissing and sharing cups, utensils, or lip balm while lesions are present
Once the sores crust over, the virus has been cleared from the body
Use a lip balm with sunscreen, because sun exposure can trigger outbreaks
Open the blisters with a clean needle so the sores dry and heal faster
The virus can be spread to others only while blisters are visible
optionRationales: Correct. Antivirals work best when started during the prodrome (tingling, burning, itching), before vesicles erupt. Starting early shortens the outbreak.
Correct. HSV-1 spreads through direct contact with lesions and saliva. Avoiding kissing and shared items while lesions are present prevents transmission.
Incorrect. HSV stays latent in the sensory nerve ganglia for life. Crusting means the outbreak is resolving, not that the virus is gone, and it can reactivate.
Correct. UV light, stress, fever, illness, and lip trauma are common triggers for reactivation. SPF lip balm reduces sun-triggered outbreaks.
Incorrect. Opening vesicles increases the risk of bacterial superinfection and of spreading the virus to the fingers (herpetic whitlow) or eyes.
Incorrect. Asymptomatic viral shedding occurs, so the virus can spread even when no lesions are visible. Hand hygiene and avoiding contact with others' mucosa remain important.
questions.rationale: Herpes simplex virus establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia and reactivates with triggers such as sun, stress, fever, and illness. Episodic antiviral therapy works best when started at the first prodromal symptoms. Teaching focuses on early treatment, trigger reduction, not touching or opening lesions, hand hygiene, and avoiding direct contact and shared items while lesions are present, remembering that shedding can occur without visible lesions.
questions.takeaway: Cold sores: treat at the first tingle, protect lips from sun, don't pop, don't share, and remember the virus stays for life.
questions.hintContent: Recall where herpes simplex virus hides between outbreaks, what triggers reactivation, and when antivirals are most effective.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each statement on its own as true or false. Be cautious with statements that describe the virus as gone or as contagious only at certain times.

questions.hintContent: Isolation for shingles depends on the client's immune status and on whether the lesions are localized or disseminated.
questions.hintStrategy: The key cue is the client's immune status. Decide whether this is the low-risk or high-risk shingles scenario before choosing precautions.
questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy for leukemia develops a painful vesicular rash along one thoracic dermatome, and the provider diagnoses herpes zoster. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Maintain standard precautions and keep the lesions covered with a dry dressing
Place the client on droplet precautions until the vesicles begin to crust
Place the client on airborne and contact precautions in a negative-pressure room
Use contact precautions only, because zoster is spread only by direct contact
optionRationales: Standard precautions with covered lesions is appropriate only for localized zoster in an immunocompetent client.
Varicella-zoster virus spreads through the air and by direct contact, not by droplets. Precautions last until all lesions are crusted, not just until crusting begins.

Correct. CDC guidance: any zoster in an immunocompromised client, or disseminated zoster in any client, needs airborne + contact precautions (negative-pressure room) until lesions are crusted or dissemination is ruled out, because the risk of dissemination and airborne spread is high.
VZV can also spread through the air, especially from immunocompromised or disseminated cases, so contact precautions alone are not enough here.
questions.rationale: Isolation for zoster depends on immune status and extent. Localized zoster in an immunocompetent client needs standard precautions with lesions covered. Immunocompromised or disseminated zoster needs airborne + contact precautions until all lesions are crusted.
questions.takeaway: Zoster + immunocompromised = airborne + contact, just like chickenpox.

An RN who recently finished chemotherapy for breast cancer
A float LPN who has never had chickenpox or the varicella vaccine
An RN who had chickenpox as a child and has documented immunity
optionRationales: Pregnant staff without proven immunity should not care for varicella clients. Congenital varicella syndrome and severe maternal pneumonia are risks.
An immunocompromised nurse is at risk of severe or disseminated infection.
A non-immune staff member would be susceptible and could become infected and spread the virus.
Correct. Only staff with documented immunity (prior disease confirmed by titer or history, or 2 vaccine doses) should care for clients with varicella.
questions.rationale: Varicella is highly contagious by the airborne route. Assign staff with documented immunity. Pregnant, immunocompromised, or non-immune staff should not be exposed.
questions.takeaway: Varicella clients get immune caregivers only.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client how to apply permethrin 5% cream for scabies. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Bathe or shower, then let the skin cool and dry completely
Apply a thin layer from the neck to the soles, including between fingers and toes and under the nails
Leave the cream on for 8 to 14 hours (usually overnight)
Wash the cream off and put on clean clothes; launder bedding and clothing in hot water
Repeat the application in about 1 week as prescribed
questions.rationale: Permethrin is applied to clean, cool, dry skin (warm skin increases absorption) from the neck down, including skin folds, finger webs, and under the nails. It stays on 8–14 hours, then is washed off. Clean clothing and hot-washed linens prevent reinfestation. A second application about 7 days later kills newly hatched mites. All close contacts are treated at the same time.
questions.takeaway: Scabies: cool dry skin → neck to soles → 8–14 hours → wash and launder → repeat in 1 week.

questions.stem: The school nurse is teaching the parents of a 7-year-old treated with permethrin 1% for head lice. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Use a fine-tooth nit comb on wet hair to remove nits
Wash bedding and hats in hot water and dry on high heat
Use a cream rinse or conditioner right before applying the lice treatment
Keep your child home from school until every nit is gone
Tell your child not to share combs, brushes, hats, or helmets
Spray the furniture and carpets with an insecticide fogger
optionRationales: Correct. Combing wet hair with a nit comb removes nits and lice that survive treatment.
Correct. Hot water (≥130°F) and high-heat drying kill lice and nits on fabric. Non-washables can be sealed in a bag for 2 weeks.
Incorrect. Conditioner coats the hair and reduces how well the pediculicide sticks and works.
Incorrect. The AAP and CDC discourage “no-nit” policies. Children can return to school after the first treatment.
Correct. Lice spread by head-to-head contact and shared personal items.
Incorrect. Fumigant sprays and foggers are not recommended. They can be toxic, and lice don't survive long off the scalp. Vacuuming is enough.
questions.rationale: Lice care combines a pediculicide, mechanical nit removal, hot laundering or bagging of personal items, and not sharing items. Household insecticides and school exclusion until nit-free are not recommended.
questions.takeaway: Lice: treat, comb, hot-wash, don't share. No foggers and no conditioner first.

Patch testing on the upper back
Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation
Punch biopsy of the lesion border
optionRationales: A Tzanck smear looks for multinucleated giant cells in herpes-virus vesicles.
Patch testing identifies type IV contact allergens.
Correct. KOH dissolves keratin in the skin scraping so fungal hyphae and spores can be seen under a microscope. It confirms tinea.
Biopsy is used to tell benign from malignant lesions. It is not the first test for a suspected fungal infection.
questions.rationale: An annular, scaly patch with central clearing that spreads among athletes in close contact suggests tinea corporis (tinea gladiatorum). Each skin test has a target. questions.stem: A client reports an itchy, red rash with small vesicles on the left wrist that is exactly the shape of the metal watch band she has worn for years. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: Irritant contact dermatitis caused by sweat and soap trapped under the band
Allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to nickel
Tinea corporis spread to the wrist from fungus living on the watch band
Atopic dermatitis triggered by the client's personal history of asthma
optionRationales: Irritant dermatitis is non-immune and usually causes diffuse dryness, burning, and cracking. It does not sharply outline an object.

Correct. A rash that exactly matches the shape of the allergen, with itching and vesicles after sensitization, is typical of allergic (type IV, T-cell-mediated) contact dermatitis. Nickel is a common cause.
Tinea forms an annular scaly patch with central clearing. It does not match an object's outline.
Atopic dermatitis typically affects flexural areas and is not shaped like a specific contact item.
questions.rationale: Allergic contact dermatitis needs prior sensitization, appears 24–72 hours after re-exposure, and takes the shape of the contact item. It is confirmed by patch testing and managed by avoidance and topical corticosteroids.
questions.takeaway: Rash in the shape of the object = allergic contact dermatitis.

questions.stem: A client with spina bifida is scheduled for surgery and reports hives and wheezing after a previous urinary catheterization. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Ask whether the client has had reactions to bananas, avocados, or kiwi
Place a latex-allergy alert band on the client and signage on the door
Request that the client be scheduled as the first surgical case of the day
Use latex gloves but premedicate the client with diphenhydramine
Obtain nonlatex catheters, gloves, tourniquets, and blood pressure cuffs
Plan to use powder-free latex gloves because they are low risk
optionRationales: Correct. Latex-fruit syndrome (banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut) is a common cross-reactivity and confirms sensitization.
Correct. Alerting all team members prevents accidental exposure.
Correct. The first case of the day lowers exposure to airborne latex particles left from earlier cases.
Incorrect. Premedication does not reliably prevent anaphylaxis. The only safe approach is avoiding latex completely.
Correct. A fully latex-free environment and supplies are needed for a client with a type I (IgE) reaction history.
Incorrect. Powder-free latex still contains latex proteins and can trigger anaphylaxis.
questions.rationale: Hives and wheezing indicate type I IgE-mediated latex allergy with anaphylaxis risk. Clients with spina bifida are high risk from repeated exposure. Management is complete latex avoidance, alerting the team, first-case scheduling, and asking about food cross-reactivity.
questions.takeaway: Latex allergy: avoid latex completely. Premedication and powder-free latex are not safe substitutes.

questions.hintContent: Eczema comes from a defective skin barrier that loses water. Think about which actions hold moisture in and which strip it away.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the parent of a 4-year-old with atopic dermatitis (eczema) on the antecubital and popliteal areas. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options: Give a long, hot bath daily with a scented bubble bath to relax the child
Rub the skin briskly with a towel after bathing to remove loose scales
Apply a thick fragrance-free emollient within 3 minutes after patting dry
Dress the child in wool clothing during winter to keep the skin warm and dry
optionRationales: Hot water and fragrance strip lipids and irritate an already defective barrier.
Brisk rubbing causes friction and itching. Skin should be patted dry.
Correct. “Soak and seal”: applying emollient within 3 minutes of bathing traps water in the skin and restores the barrier. This is the foundation of eczema care.
Wool is a common irritant and itch trigger. Soft cotton is preferred.
questions.rationale: Atopic dermatitis comes from a defective skin barrier. Short lukewarm baths, mild cleansers, patting dry, and immediate emollients reduce flares. Avoid irritants like wool, fragrance, and heat.
questions.takeaway: Eczema: lukewarm soak, pat, seal within 3 minutes.

questions.stem: A client with plaque psoriasis covering 20% of the body surface is to start a biologic agent (a TNF inhibitor). Which action should the nurse verify before the first dose?
options: The client has received the live intranasal influenza vaccine this week
A tuberculosis screening test result is negative
The client has stopped all topical emollients
A skin biopsy of a plaque has been completed
optionRationales: Live vaccines are contraindicated during biologic therapy and should be given well before starting, not just before the first dose.
Correct. TNF inhibitors and other biologics suppress immunity and can reactivate latent TB. A negative TB test (IGRA or PPD) is required before starting.
Emollients remain an important add-on in psoriasis and don't need to be stopped.
A biopsy is not required when the clinical diagnosis of plaque psoriasis is clear.
questions.rationale: Biologic immunomodulators raise the risk of serious infection, especially latent TB reactivation. Screening for TB and hepatitis, and avoiding live vaccines, are key safety steps.
questions.takeaway: Before any biologic: TB test first.

options: allergic
irritant
atopic
seborrheic
is a non-immune reaction from direct damage to the skin
requires prior sensitization to an antigen
is an IgE-mediated immediate reaction
is caused by a dermatophyte fungus
switching to hot water to remove residue
using alcohol-based hand rub when hands are not visibly soiled and applying facility-approved moisturizer
wearing latex gloves for all tasks
skipping hand hygiene between clients until healed

questions.rationale: Frequent soap and water damages the skin barrier directly without an immune process. This is irritant contact dermatitis, which can occur without prior sensitization. Alcohol-based rubs with emollients are less damaging than repeated washing. Regular moisturizing restores the barrier, and hand hygiene must never be skipped.
questions.takeaway: Frequent washing + chapped hands = irritant dermatitis. Use alcohol rub plus moisturizer.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with dark skin asks where to focus a monthly skin self-examination for melanoma. Which response is most accurate?
options: “Check your palms, the soles of your feet, and under your nails for new dark spots.”
“Focus mainly on your face, ears, and neck, because those areas get the most sun.”
“Darker skin can't develop melanoma, so you only need to check for new moles once a year.”
“Check only the areas that itch, since melanoma nearly always causes itching first.”
optionRationales: Correct. Acral lentiginous melanoma, the most common melanoma subtype in people with darker skin, appears on the palms, soles, and nail beds (a new dark streak in the nail).
Sun-exposed areas matter, but in darker skin melanoma often appears on areas that get little sun, so limiting the exam to the face, ears, and neck would miss it.
People with dark skin do get melanoma, and it is often diagnosed later and at a more advanced stage.
Melanoma is often painless and not itchy. Relying on itching would delay detection.
questions.rationale: All skin tones need skin self-examination and sun protection. In darker skin, melanoma is disproportionately acral, so teaching must include the palms, soles, nail beds, and mucous membranes.
questions.takeaway: Dark skin: check palms, soles, and nails for melanoma.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a group of lifeguards about preventing skin cancer. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “Use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher.”
“Water-resistant sunscreen lasts all day, so reapply it only if you towel off.”
“A base tan from a tanning bed before summer will protect you from burns.”
“Sunscreen is only necessary on sunny days when you can feel the heat.”
“Wear a wide-brimmed hat and UV-blocking sunglasses, and seek shade between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.”
“Examine your skin monthly and report any mole that is changing in size, shape, or color.”
optionRationales: Correct. The AAD recommends broad-spectrum (UVA/UVB), water-resistant SPF ≥30.
Incorrect. Water resistance lasts only 40 or 80 minutes. Sunscreen should be reapplied at least every 2 hours and right after swimming, sweating, or towel drying.
Incorrect. Tanning beds increase melanoma risk, and there is no safe “base tan.”
Incorrect. UV rays penetrate clouds and cause damage regardless of heat.
Correct. Physical barriers and avoiding peak UV hours reduce exposure.
Correct. Monthly self-exam finds evolving lesions (the E in ABCDE) early.
questions.rationale: Sun protection combines broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF ≥30, reapplied at least every 2 hours and after water), shade, clothing, hats, sunglasses, avoiding tanning beds, and regular skin self-exams. Common myths (base tans, cloudy-day safety, all-day water resistance) need correcting.
questions.takeaway: SPF 30+, reapply every 2 hours, shade from 10 to 4, no tanning beds, check monthly.
